info.name: Lab 5 demo (Team 14)
info.description: The Lab 5 demo, one folder per grade, in the order it is presented. Send the requests top to bottom; steps marked MANUAL: are done by hand (terminal, Docker Desktop): their description says what to do. Run folder 0 first: it creates the demo player and its token.

item.name: 0. Before the demo
item.description:
Run these once, about 10 minutes before presenting. They check the stack is up
and create the demo player whose token the other folders use.

Select the environment that holds this stack's keys (brokerKey, adminKey,
gatewayKey) first: the defaults here are the `.env.example` placeholders.

item.name: MANUAL: Start the stack, check Docker Desktop

request.description:
In PowerShell, in `pad-team-14-tamagotchi-go`:

    docker compose up -d

Then Docker Desktop -> Containers -> `tamagotchi-go`: nothing should be
"Restarting". Every pgpool now waits for its three Postgres nodes, so a cold
start should be clean. If a service still loops on "pgpool is not accepting any
new connections" or stops at "waiting for migration lock", restart its pgpool,
then the service, e.g.:

    docker compose restart package-registry-service-db
    docker compose restart package-registry-service

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Gateway is up
Message Broker is up
ETL service is up
Register the demo player

request.description: A new player for this demo. Registration and login need no token.

exec: // A new name every send, so the demo can be run again.

item.name: Log in: the token for the next requests
Grades 2 and 3 - The architecture diagram
MANUAL: Open the diagram

request.description:
Open `docs/images/architecture.png` (or the README's "Architecture Diagram"
section on GitHub, `dev` branch). Point at, in order:

1. API Gateway: the single entry point.
2. Message Broker, and inside it the Saga coordinator and its SQLite store.
3. Service Discovery, ws-proxy, monitoring (Prometheus, Loki, Grafana).
4. Every service with its replicas.
5. Every data store: PostgreSQL x3 behind pgpool, Redis x3, and the
   replication note (repmgr, 3 shared Sentinels, quorum 2).   <- grade 3
6. cache-1, cache-2, cache-3: the shared cache on the hash ring.     <- grade 3
7. ETL service and Data Warehouse.                                   <- grade 3

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Grade 5 - Replication and failover
item.description:
User Management's PostgreSQL: three nodes under repmgr behind pgpool
(`user-management-service-db`). Registering a player is a write, so it must
reach the primary: it shows the failover directly (no cache in between).

item.name: MANUAL: Who is the primary

request.description:
In PowerShell:

    docker compose exec -u 1001 user-management-service-db-1 /opt/bitnami/scripts/postgresql-repmgr/entrypoint.sh repmgr -f /opt/bitnami/repmgr/conf/repmgr.conf cluster show

One `primary`, two `standby`. Note which node is the primary.

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Register a player (a write, to the primary)

exec: // A new name every send, so the demo can be run again.

item.name: MANUAL: Stop the primary

request.description:
Docker Desktop -> `tamagotchi-go` -> press **Stop** on the node that
`cluster show` named primary (e.g. `user-management-service-db-0`).

Then go straight on to the next request.

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Register a player during the failover

request.description:
Send it right after stopping the primary, and again until it is 201.
For a few seconds, while repmgr promotes a standby, the service answers
503 + Retry-After: 2 (a write in flight is not repeated blindly). Measured:
two 503s, then every write 201.

exec: // A new name every send, so the demo can be run again.
pm.test('503 + Retry-After: the database is failing over, send again in 2 s', () =>
pm.test('201 Created: the write reached the new primary', () => pm.response.to.have.status(201));

item.name: Log in as that player (a read from the new primary)

exec: pm.test('200 OK: the player written during the failover is there', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: MANUAL: Who is the primary now

request.description:
In PowerShell, against a node that is still running (not the one you stopped):

    docker compose exec -u 1001 user-management-service-db-1 /opt/bitnami/scripts/postgresql-repmgr/entrypoint.sh repmgr -f /opt/bitnami/repmgr/conf/repmgr.conf cluster show
    docker compose exec -u 1001 user-management-service-db-2 /opt/bitnami/scripts/postgresql-repmgr/entrypoint.sh repmgr -f /opt/bitnami/repmgr/conf/repmgr.conf cluster show

The stopped node is `failed`; a former standby is now `primary`.

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: MANUAL: Start the old primary again

request.description:
Docker Desktop -> press **Start** on the node you stopped. After about 40 s:

    docker compose exec -u 1001 user-management-service-db-1 /opt/bitnami/scripts/postgresql-repmgr/entrypoint.sh repmgr -f /opt/bitnami/repmgr/conf/repmgr.conf cluster show

It is back as a `standby` of the new primary: it rejoined by itself.

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: MANUAL: Redis too: master, 2 replicas, 3 Sentinels

request.description:
In PowerShell:

    docker compose exec redis-sentinel-1 redis-cli -p 26379 sentinel get-master-addr-by-name monster-raid-service-cache

Stop `monster-raid-service-cache` in Docker Desktop, run it again: within
about 5 s the address is a replica's (the Sentinels promoted it). Start the old
one again: about 15 s later it is a replica of the new master.
Every group at once: `docker compose exec redis-sentinel-1 redis-cli -p 26379 sentinel masters`

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Grade 6 - Caching
item.description:
Commonly read GETs and authentication data come from the shared cache nodes.
Every cached read says where it came from in the X-Cache response header:
`miss` (the database, now cached) or `hit` (the cache). Open the response's
Headers tab.

item.name: My profile, first read (X-Cache: miss)

exec: pm.test('X-Cache: miss - read from the database, now cached', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('X-Cache')).to.eql('miss'));

item.name: My profile again (X-Cache: hit)

exec: pm.test('X-Cache: hit - read from the cache', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('X-Cache')).to.eql('hit'));

item.name: Setup: a package the demo player moderates

request.description: Registered by the stack's seeded admin, with the demo player as its moderator.

item.name: The package, first read (X-Cache: miss)
The package again (X-Cache: hit)
Change it (the write deletes the cached copy)

request.description: After the database commit, Package Registry deletes the package's cache key.

item.name: The package after the change (X-Cache: miss, new value)

exec: pm.test('X-Cache: miss - the write deleted the cached copy', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('X-Cache')).to.eql('miss'));
pm.test('the new value, not a stale one', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().statDefinitions.hunger.bonusMultiplier).to.eql(1.5));

item.name: Auth data: the gateway's verified-token cache

request.description:
Every request above with a Bearer token was checked by the gateway once
(signature), then found in the cache (`gateway:token:<sha256>`, until the
token's exp, at most 5 min). The log shows it too:

    docker compose logs --since 5m gateway | Select-String "cache (hit|miss)"

exec: pm.test('token cache hits are counted', () => pm.expect(rows.some(l => l.includes('result="hit"'))).to.be.true);

item.name: Grade 7 - Consistent hashing and the sharded cache
item.description:
Every key goes to one of cache-1..3, picked by our consistent-hash ring
(FNV-1a + fmix32, 160 virtual nodes per node), the same in TypeScript, Go and
Python. The research: README, "Cache Sharding with Consistent Hashing".

item.name: Every cache node is in use (all services, from Prometheus)

request.description: Prometheus adds up cache_requests_total from every replica of every service, per cache node: all three nodes get traffic.

item.name: MANUAL: Keys spread over the three nodes

request.description:
In PowerShell, in `pad-team-14-tamagotchi-go`:

    $p = (Select-String '^CACHE_PASSWORD=' .env).Line.Split('=',2)[1]
    foreach ($n in 'cache-1','cache-2','cache-3') { "$n : $(docker compose exec $n valkey-cli -a $p --no-auth-warning dbsize)" }

Each node holds a share. The keys on one node, from several services:

    docker compose exec cache-2 valkey-cli -a $p --no-auth-warning --scan

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: MANUAL: Why a ring: measured

request.description:
In PowerShell, in `pad-team-14-tamagotchi-go\hash-ring`:

    npm install
    npm run stats

With 1 virtual node the split is about 5% / 34% / 61%; with 160, a third
each. Adding a 4th node moves about 25% of the keys on the ring, against 75%
with `hash mod N`. The three ports agree on one file of test vectors:
`cd python; python -m unittest -v`.

exec: pm.test('Do this step by hand: see the description', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));

item.name: Grade 9 - Long-running sagas, coordinator in the Message Broker
item.description:
The coordinator runs each saga's steps in order (POST /saga-steps on each
service). If a step says no, it undoes the finished steps in reverse order.
Here: raid-activation = Package Registry `mark-activating` -> Monster Raid
`create-raid` -> Package Registry `activate`.

item.name: A draft raid config
Rollback: a raid Monster Raid rejects (maxHp 0)

request.description:
Started on the coordinator directly, with a raid Monster Raid must refuse.
Step 1 marks the config `activating`; step 2 answers 422; the coordinator
compensates step 1 (the config goes back to `draft`); step 3 never runs.

exec: pm.test('step 1 undone, step 2 rejected, step 3 never ran', () =>

item.name: Activate the same config the normal way

request.description: After the rollback the config is a draft again, so it can be activated. Package Registry starts the raid-activation saga on the broker.

exec: pm.test('the raid is active: ' + body.raidId, () => pm.expect(body.status).to.eql('active'));

Every saga so far
